articles.headline: Plant-Based Meats All Contained Fungal Toxins. Here's What to Know
articles.body: Every single one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives tested in a UK study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin. The good news? Concentrations remained below European guideline limits. But this matters for how you think about ultra-processed meat substitutes. Most plant-based options rely on fermentation and processing to achieve that meaty texture and shelf stability—conditions where mycotoxins can develop. If you're leaning on these products as your primary protein source, the study suggests rotating in whole foods: legumes, nuts, tempeh, and properly sourced tofu. The point isn't to panic; it's to understand what's in your ultra-processed foods, whether they're conventional or alternative.
articles.takeaway: Plant-based meats are convenient but not perfect. Build your protein strategy around whole foods and use processed options as rotation, not the foundation.

articles.topic: Vitamin D boosts cognitive test scores
articles.headline: 5,000 IU Daily Vitamin D Improved Cognitive Performance by 13% in Older Adults
articles.body: A new study found something straightforward: older adults with mild cognitive impairment and sleep problems who took at least 5,000 IU of vitamin D daily scored more than 13% higher on cognitive tests compared to those taking none. That's meaningful. Vitamin D isn't glamorous, but it regulates calcium absorption, supports immune function, and crosses the blood-brain barrier. If you're over 50, live somewhere with seasonal darkness, or spend most time indoors, you're probably deficient. The study didn't look at mega-doses; it was the baseline clinical dose. Talk to your doctor about your levels. But here's the insight: cognitive performance in aging isn't just about supplements. It's about sleep quality, movement, and foundational micronutrients your brain literally can't optimize without.
articles.takeaway: If you have mild cognitive issues or poor sleep, get your vitamin D checked and consider supplementing at clinical doses under medical guidance.

articles.topic: Slow breathing changes heart activity and risk tolerance
articles.headline: Slow Breathing Actually Rewires How Your Brain Handles Risk
articles.body: Here's something counterintuitive: slow breathing with a prolonged exhale doesn't just calm you down—it changes how your heart communicates with your brain and literally increases your willingness to take risks. The mechanism is elegant. Slow, deep breaths reduce heart rate variability, which signals safety to your nervous system. But this also increases the brain's sensitivity to reward signals. That means you're more likely to take calculated risks when calm than when anxious. The implications flip conventional wisdom on its head. Before a big meeting or decision, a five-minute breathing protocol isn't just stress relief—it's tactical. You're resetting your risk-reward perception. The research suggests that breath work isn't primarily about relaxation; it's about recalibrating how your brain processes opportunity versus threat. That's a tool.
articles.takeaway: Use slow, extended-exhale breathing before decisions or high-stakes moments. You'll be calmer and think more clearly about opportunity, not just threat.

articles.headline: A New Heart Disease Framework Changes Everything About Prevention
articles.body: The American Heart Association just introduced something significant: cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, which reframes how doctors think about heart disease. Instead of isolated conditions, this recognizes that your heart, kidneys, and metabolism are one system. The data is striking: fewer than 11% of US adults meet criteria for optimal CKM health. Meanwhile, nearly 15% have advanced multisystem disease. Here's why this matters for you. Traditional risk factors—cholesterol, blood pressure—miss the bigger picture. CKM syndrome catches people earlier, when intervention still works. The framework suggests that if your blood sugar is creeping up, your blood pressure is borderline, and you're gaining weight, these aren't separate problems. They're one problem with one solution: sustained behavioral change. The good news? The AHA's Life's Essential 8 (better eating, more movement, quit tobacco, better sleep, healthy weight, controlled cholesterol, managed blood sugar, managed blood pressure) could prevent 40% of cardiovascular deaths if adopted widely.
articles.takeaway: Don't treat heart disease risk factors in isolation. See them as interconnected. If one marker is off, you need systemic change, not a single medication.

workout.title: Short Stride Acceleration: 30/30 Intro to Speed
workout.tip: Focus on smooth arm drive and controlled breathing during the 30-second push—don't sprint all-out. Your recovery jog should feel easy; if you can't talk, you're recovering too hard.
workout.warmup: 5 min: easy jog at conversational pace, then 6 x 20m strides with 40m walk recovery between each (stride should feel controlled, not maximal—build into it)

exercises.name: 30/30 Interval Block
exercises.notes: Run at a pace you could sustain for about 3-4 minutes (roughly 85–90% max effort). Keep your head still, shoulders relaxed, and cadence quick. Recovery jog should feel genuinely easy—this teaches your body pacing discipline.

workout.cooldown: 3 min easy jog, then 2 min stationary walk. Standing quad stretch 20 sec each leg, standing hamstring reach 20 sec each leg, open hip stretch 15 sec each side.
workout.description: Your first exposure to running speed work using safe, short 30-second efforts followed by 30-second recovery jogs. This session teaches your nervous system to move faster without the injury risk of longer intervals, making it perfect for 5K and 10K beginners building speed foundations.

meal.title: Spaghetti al Pomodoro with Sardines, Garlic & Chili Flake
meal.description: A fast, Mediterranean-Italian pasta with canned sardines, fresh tomato, and garlic—complete protein, omega-3s, and quick carbs in under 20 minutes. Perfect for the endurance athlete who needs dinner fast without sacrificing nutrition.
ingredients: 1 can (3.75 oz) sardines in water, drained
meal.instructions:
1. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add spaghetti and cook until al dente, about 9–10 minutes. Reserve 0.5 cup pasta water before draining.
2. While pasta cooks, heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add sliced garlic and red chili flake. Cook for 1–2 minutes until fragrant but not brown.
3. Pour in crushed tomatoes and salt. Simmer for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. The sauce should smell sweet and alive.
4. Gently break sardines into the sauce and fold in. Warm through for 1 minute—don't break them into tiny pieces.
5. Add drained spaghetti directly to the sauce. Toss gently. Add pasta water in small splashes until the sauce coats the noodles but still pools slightly on the plate.
6. Top with fresh parsley and a crack of black pepper. Squeeze lemon juice over the top just before eating.
meal.tip: Sardines are one of the most nutrient-dense foods on the planet for endurance athletes—loaded with protein, omega-3s, calcium, and iron. Keep a few cans in your pantry for weeknight wins. This dish is best eaten fresh, but leftovers reheat gently with a splash of water on low heat.
